opus-5.5.text:
I think the key distinction is between algorithmic progress that's essentially "free," meaning insights you can get from cognitive labor alone, like thinking harder, writing better code, or coming up with a cleverer idea on a whiteboard, and algorithmic progress that's bottlenecked on compute and experimentation.

When people imagine automating AI research, they often picture the first kind. You spin up millions of copies of an AI researcher, they think really fast, and algorithmic progress explodes. But when you look at how algorithmic improvements have actually come about over the past decade, a large share of them seem tied to scale. Many innovations only show their value, or only become discoverable, when you run experiments at substantial compute budgets. Things like the right architecture choices, scaling recipes, data mixtures, and training stability tricks often need to be validated empirically at meaningful scale, and some techniques that look good at small scale don't transfer.

So if a big fraction of algorithmic progress is complementary to compute rather than substitutable for it, then automating the researchers alone doesn't give you an unbounded speedup. You get a speedup on the cognitive-labor portion, but you're still constrained by how many experiments you can run, how large they are, and how quickly you can get hardware. That's an Amdahl's-law-style argument. The part you can't accelerate ends up dominating.

That's why I tend to be more skeptical of very fast software-only intelligence explosion scenarios. I don't think the effect is zero. Automated researchers could make much better use of a given compute budget, choose experiments more wisely, and extract more from small-scale runs. But how much of algorithmic progress is "ideas-limited" versus "experiment-limited" is, to me, one of the most important empirical questions for figuring out how fast things could go once AI research is automated.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts cognitive-labor-driven progress with compute- and experiment-limited progress; it does not distinguish expanding the capability frontier from reducing the cost of existing capabilities.

r002.rationale: It does not suggest that cost reductions are easier to achieve than frontier expansion.

r003.rationale: It does not explain how cheaper models could enable more inference compute and thereby improve capabilities.

r004.rationale: The response says software-only acceleration is limited when progress depends on compute and experiments, but does not make the specified judgment about weaker capability feedback when algorithmic progress primarily reduces costs.

fable-5.1.text:
The distinction I keep coming back to is between the kind of algorithmic progress that is cheap to find and the kind that is expensive to find. When people talk about automating AI research, they often imagine that if you have a system that can do the work of a thousand researchers, you'll get a thousand times the rate of progress. But that assumes the bottleneck is researcher hours, and I don't think that's quite right.

A lot of the algorithmic improvements we've seen historically have been things you can discover at small scale and then extrapolate: better optimizers, normalization tricks, architectural tweaks, data filtering improvements. Those are relatively cheap in compute terms. You run a bunch of experiments on small models, you find what works, and you scale it up. If that's where most of the gains are, then automating the research labor really does help a lot, because the binding constraint is coming up with ideas and running lots of small experiments quickly.

But there's another category of progress that only shows up at scale, where you can't tell whether a change helps until you've spent a substantial fraction of a frontier training run on it. Things like how to allocate compute between pretraining and post-training, how certain capabilities emerge, or whether a technique that works at a billion parameters still works at a trillion. For that category, the bottleneck isn't cognitive labor at all. It's compute for experimentation. You could have a million automated researchers and they'd still be waiting in line for the same cluster.

So when I assess how much automated AI research would accelerate things, the question I'm really asking is: what fraction of the historical gains in algorithmic efficiency came from the first bucket versus the second? Our estimates suggest that algorithmic progress has been contributing roughly as much as compute scaling to effective capability gains, maybe a doubling of effective compute every eight months or so. But that headline number hides the composition. If most of it was cheap-to-find, then automation gives you a big multiplier. If a lot of it required expensive, large-scale experimentation, then the multiplier is much smaller, and you end up in a world where progress is still fundamentally gated by how much hardware you can throw at experiments.

I think the honest answer is that it's a mix, and we have fairly wide uncertainty about the proportions. But that distinction, between labor-constrained and compute-constrained algorithmic progress, is doing most of the work in my overall view on how explosive the feedback loop could be.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes algorithmic improvements by how costly they are to discover and test, not by whether they expand capabilities or reduce the cost of existing capabilities.

r002.rationale: It says some improvements can be found with small-scale experiments, but does not compare cost reductions with expansion of the capability frontier.

r003.rationale: The response does not explain how cheaper models could enable more inference compute and thereby improve capabilities.

r004.rationale: It says acceleration would be smaller when progress requires expensive, large-scale experiments, but does not judge the feedback case as weaker when progress primarily reduces costs.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish between algorithmic progress that makes a given capability cheaper and progress that lets us achieve capabilities we couldn’t achieve before. You might find a more efficient way to train a model and get the same performance with less compute. Or you might discover a method that pushes performance beyond what was previously possible, even with a large compute budget.

That distinction matters for automated AI research because making existing systems cheaper doesn’t necessarily make them better researchers. It could still accelerate research by letting you run more experiments or more copies of an AI researcher. But improvements that make those systems better at research could create a more direct feedback loop: better AI researchers develop better methods, which produce still better AI researchers.

So I’d be cautious about taking a measured rate of algorithmic efficiency improvement and treating it as the rate at which automated research capability will improve. They’re related, but they’re not the same thing.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes making the same capability cheaper from achieving capabilities that were previously out of reach.

r002.rationale: It does not compare how easy it is to reduce costs versus expand the capability frontier.

r003.rationale: It says cheaper systems could accelerate research by allowing more experiments or copies of an AI researcher, conveying an indirect benefit from running more of them.

r004.rationale: It says cost reductions do not necessarily make systems better researchers and contrasts them with improvements that create a more direct feedback loop.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is between algorithmic progress that makes AI systems more computationally efficient and progress that makes them more capable. You might discover a way to reach the same level of performance using much less compute. That’s valuable, but it doesn’t necessarily mean you can push beyond the capabilities of the best existing systems.

For automated AI research, we need to understand whether AI can do both: find efficiency improvements and develop ideas that advance the frontier. Evidence that systems can optimize an existing training setup is encouraging, but it doesn’t, by itself, establish that they can automate the research needed to build substantially more capable successors.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes efficiency improvements that achieve the same performance with less compute from progress that advances the capability frontier.

r002.rationale: It says efficiency gains do not necessarily push beyond current capabilities, but does not suggest they are easier to achieve than frontier-expanding progress.

r003.rationale: It does not explain that lower costs can enable more inference compute and thereby indirectly improve capabilities.

r004.rationale: It says efficiency gains alone do not establish automated development of more capable successors, but does not assess the strength of an accelerated capability feedback loop.
